SOAP Clinical Note

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint: 3-day history of diarrhea (4–5 watery/loose stools per day) with mild intermittent abdominal pain and one episode of vomiting. Slight subjective fever, decreased appetite, able to maintain oral fluid intake. No blood or mucus in stool. No recent travel or unusual food exposure.
- Past medical history: Asthma (childhood/on-going).
- Medications:
  • “Laxepro” (patient reports yellow inhaler) – dose/route/frequency not documented.  (Name uncertain; see quality check.)
  • No OTC or other prescribed drugs taken for current episode.
- Allergies: Denies any drug or food allergies.
- Family history: Father had hypertension and died of bowel cancer at age 62.
- Social history: Not discussed.

Objective:
- Telehealth visual assessment: Patient appears well hydrated; no overt signs of dehydration noted by clinician (e.g., mucous membranes appear moist, alert).
- No vital signs or in-person physical examination performed.
- No investigations performed.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Acute diarrhea
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Self-limiting viral or non-specific gastroenteritis.
   - Differential diagnosis: Bacterial enteritis, food-borne illness, inflammatory bowel disease flare (less likely).
   - Investigations planned: None at this time; stool culture if diarrhea persists >7 days or if blood/mucus appears.
   - Treatment planned:
     • Oral rehydration solution (e.g., OTC Dioralyte) to replace fluids and electrolytes.
     • Soft, easily digestible diet: crackers, toast, jam, mashed boiled vegetables. Avoid dairy (except yogurt), meat, fish, and eggs until 48 hrs after complete resolution of diarrhea.
     • Introduce yogurt/probiotics to restore gut flora.
   - Follow-up: Seek medical review if stools increase to ≥6–8/day, signs of dehydration emerge, bloody stools develop, or symptoms last >1 week.

Quality checks:
• Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs; complete medication list with doses; smoking/alcohol history; surgical history; review of systems; objective abdominal examination.
• Internal conflicts: Medication name “Laxepro” reported as an inhaler; “Lexapro” is typically an oral antidepressant—not an inhaler (conflict noted).
• Transcript quality: Clear overall; minor inaudible segments around medication name.
